---
title: "10-minute quickstart"
subtitle: "From zero to arrays, compute and tables"
---

This tour takes you through the essentials of Marrow from Python: building
arrays, running compute kernels, and assembling columns into a table. Every
snippet on this page is executed when the docs are built, so the output you see
is real.

## Install

Marrow is a Mojo project with a Python binding compiled to a native extension.
Clone the repository and build the extension with [pixi](https://pixi.sh):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kszucs/marrow
cd marrow
pixi run build_python     # compiles the native extension (python/marrow/libmarrow.so)
```

Then make it importable and bring it in under the customary `ma` alias:

```{python}
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "../../python")   # point at the built extension
import marrow as ma
```

::: {.callout-tip}
The API deliberately mirrors [PyArrow](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/).
If you know `pa.array`, `pa.record_batch` and `pa.table`, you already know most
of Marrow.
:::

## Create an array

`ma.array()` turns a Python list into a columnar array. The type is inferred in
a single pass, and `None` marks a null position:

```{python}
a = ma.array([1, 2, 3, None, 5])
print(a)
print("length:    ", len(a))
print("null count:", a.null_count())
print("type:      ", a.type())
```

Pass `type=` to skip inference and coerce the data to a specific type — this is
also the fastest path:

```{python}
f = ma.array([1, 2, 3], type=ma.float32())
print(f)
```

Strings, nested lists and structs all work the same way:

```{python}
print(ma.array(["hello", None, "world"]))
print(ma.array([[1, 2], [3, 4, 5], None]))
print(ma.array([{"x": 1, "y": 1.5}, {"x": 2, "y": 2.5}]))
```

## Compute on arrays

Compute kernels are vectorized and null-aware, and the names mirror
`pyarrow.compute`. A null in either operand propagates to the result:

```{python}
x = ma.array([1, 2, 3, None, 5])
y = ma.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])

print("add:     ", ma.add(x, y))        # index 3 is null
print("multiply:", ma.multiply(y, y))
```

Aggregates reduce an array to a scalar and **skip** nulls:

```{python}
print("sum:", ma.sum(x))
print("min:", ma.min(x))
print("max:", ma.max(x))
```

Comparisons return a boolean array, which you can feed straight into `filter`:

```{python}
big  = ma.greater(y, ma.array([15, 15, 15, 15, 15]))
print("mask:  ", big)
print("kept:  ", ma.filter(y, big))
print("no nulls:", ma.drop_null(x))
```

Sorting handles nulls explicitly and returns either the sorted values or the
sort indices:

```{python}
s = ma.array([3, 1, None, 2, 5])
print("sorted:  ", ma.sort(s))
print("desc:    ", ma.sort(s, ascending=False, null_placement="at_end"))
print("argsort: ", s.argsort())
```

## Assemble a table

A `RecordBatch` is a schema plus a set of equal-length columns — the workhorse
tabular structure:

```{python}
people = ma.record_batch({
    "name":   ma.array(["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"]),
    "age":    ma.array([34, 28, 45, 52]),
    "salary": ma.array([95_000, 72_000, 120_000, 88_000]),
})
print(people)
print("shape:", people.shape())
```

Inspect it as native Python with `to_pydict()` (column-oriented) or
`to_pylist()` (row-oriented):

```{python}
print(people.to_pydict())
print(people.to_pylist())
```

Select columns, slice rows, and sort by one or more keys:

```{python}
print(people.select(["name", "salary"]).to_pydict())
print(people.slice(1, 2).to_pylist())
print(people.sort_by([("age", "descending")]).to_pylist())
```
